title: Distributed execution: partitions, shuffles and what actually ran
summary: Read a Spark plan, predict its shuffle boundaries and stages, then compare the prediction with measured tasks, shuffle records, skew and adaptive changes from a recorded local run.
objectives: Predict Exchange nodes, stages and task counts from a physical plan and check them against a recorded local run.
Explain with numbers why one hot key defeats extra workers and extra partitions, and what a broadcast, a salt, adaptive execution or a cache changes.
Separate what a toy local run proves from what only a measurement at real size can show.

questions.prompt: The grouped sum by plant is run again over a feed with 840 rows in four input partitions, still with four shuffle partitions and adaptive execution off. How many Exchange nodes and executed stages does its plan have?

options.text: One Exchange and two stages: the plan depends on the operators and settings, not on the row count.
options.rationale: The exchange comes from the grouped operator; stage counts follow shuffle boundaries and the partition settings, so 840 rows change nothing here.

options.text: Two Exchanges, because more rows need a second redistribution.
options.rationale: Row volume does not add operators; Spark plans one hash-partitioned exchange for one grouped aggregation regardless of size.

options.text: Zero Exchanges, because a sum is computed inside each partition.
options.rationale: The partial sums do run inside partitions, but the final sum per plant still needs every plant's partials in one place, which is the exchange.

options.text: It cannot be predicted without running, because plans are only known at runtime.
options.rationale: Adaptive execution can revise a plan at runtime, but it was off here and the exchange count is visible before any action.

questions.prompt: After repartition(16, "plant") on the skewed feed the largest partition still holds 180 rows. A colleague proposes repartition(64, "plant") to fix the slow task. What will the measurement show?

options.text: About 45 rows in the largest partition, because four times more partitions means a quarter of the work each.
options.rationale: That arithmetic holds for many evenly spread keys; the rows of a single key never divide across hash partitions.

options.text: The largest partition still holds at least the 180 North rows; hash partitioning by plant cannot split one key.
options.rationale: Every row with the same key hashes to the same partition, so the hot key sets a floor that no partition count moves.

options.text: The rows spread evenly because Spark balances partitions automatically when a count is given.
options.rationale: A partition count sets how many hash buckets exist, not how keys are assigned to them; balancing happens only with a round-robin repartition and no key.

options.text: Most partitions are empty and the job fails with an out of memory error.
options.rationale: Empty partitions are normal and harmless; nothing about a larger partition count causes a failure on 240 rows.

questions.prompt: A notebook calls collect() on the 240-row fact frame to sum inspected units in Python. Which statement about that choice is correct?

options.text: It fails immediately for any DataFrame because collect() is only allowed on aggregates.
options.rationale: collect() is allowed on any DataFrame; the risk is the size of what arrives, not a rule that forbids it.

options.text: It is the recommended way because the driver is the fastest process in the application.
options.rationale: The driver coordinates work; it is one process with one heap and is the place a large collection exhausts memory.

options.text: It works for 240 rows but would move every row into the driver's memory for a large feed; sum the column in Spark and collect the one-row result instead.
options.rationale: collect() serializes all rows to one process; an aggregate computed by the executors and then collected moves a bounded result.

options.text: It is safe because count() ran first and counted the rows without moving them.
options.rationale: count() moving nothing to the driver says nothing about the cost of a later collect() of the same rows.

cards.prompt: What does the driver do that an executor never does?
cards.answer: It holds the session, builds the plan, splits it into stages and tasks, and schedules those tasks on executors.
cards.explanation: Executors run tasks and hold partitions; the driver coordinates. In local[2] both roles live in one JVM with two task slots, which is why a local run can show every mechanism but no realistic speed.

cards.prompt: Why can explain() print a plan before any row is computed?
cards.answer: Transformations only extend a lazy plan; execution starts when an action such as collect, count or a write asks for output.
cards.explanation: Because nothing runs until an action, you can read the proposed operators, count the exchanges and predict the stages before paying for a task. The lab wrapped explain() in its own job group and counted zero jobs.

cards.prompt: How are partitions and tasks related within one stage?
cards.answer: A stage runs exactly one task per partition of its input, so 240 rows in four partitions means four tasks for a filter.
cards.explanation: The partition count decides parallelism: four partitions cannot use more than four task slots at once, and one oversized partition becomes one long task however many slots exist.

cards.prompt: Predict the plan of a filter followed by a select over a partitioned frame.
cards.answer: Project over Filter over Scan with no Exchange: each output partition depends on one input partition, so the chain runs in one stage.
cards.explanation: That is a narrow dependency. The lab measured one job, one stage and four tasks for it; rows kept per partition were 47, 48, 45 and 47, exactly each input slice's defective rows, because nothing moved.

cards.prompt: Which operator marks a shuffle in a physical plan, and what crossed it in the grouped sum?
cards.answer: Exchange; for the grouped sum it carried twelve partial rows, one per plant from each of four input partitions, not the 240 raw rows.
cards.explanation: The partial HashAggregate below the Exchange sums inside each task first, so only partials cross hashpartitioning(plant#1, 4). The reduce tasks then read 8, 0, 4 and 0 of those records. Every Exchange ends a stage.

cards.prompt: Why did the second stage of the grouped sum run four tasks when two of them read nothing?
cards.answer: Because spark.sql.shuffle.partitions was 4 and adaptive execution was off; a stage reading a shuffle has that many tasks whatever the data.
cards.explanation: The setting, not the data, fixed the task count: three plants hashed into two of the four shuffle partitions. With adaptive execution on, the same shuffle was read as one coalesced partition by a single task.

cards.prompt: What changed in the plan and in the shuffled records when the plant dimension was broadcast?
cards.answer: SortMergeJoin with three Exchanges became BroadcastHashJoin with one Exchange and one BroadcastExchange; shuffled records fell from 243 plus 3 partials to 8 partials.
cards.explanation: A separate one-task job computed the three-row dimension; the driver collected it and shipped one copy to every executor, where the fact tasks shared it, so the 240 fact rows never crossed a shuffle and the join ran inside the scanning task. Measured stages went from 1, 4, 4, 4 to 1, 4, 4.

cards.prompt: Give a concrete counterexample to the claim that more workers are always faster.
cards.answer: A stage whose partitions hold 204, 36, 0 and 0 rows: the second slot idles after 36 rows while the first works to 204, and extra slots idle from the start.
cards.explanation: The lab measured that distribution after repartition(4, "plant") on the skewed feed. A stage ends when its longest task ends, and hash partitioning kept all 180 North rows in one task at 8 and 16 partitions too.

cards.prompt: Why does a round-robin repartition(16) before a window by plant not fix the slow task?
cards.answer: The window needs every row of one plant together, so its own hashpartitioning(plant) exchange follows the round-robin one and re-collects the hot key.
cards.explanation: The plan kept both exchanges, the job shuffled 480 records instead of 240, and the busiest window task still read 204 rows. The extra shuffle cost a full pass over the data and changed nothing about the key.

cards.prompt: How does salting a join key split a hot key without changing the answer?
cards.answer: Add salt = crc32(event_id) % 4 to the facts, replicate the small side once per salt, and join on (plant, salt): each fact row still meets exactly one replica.
cards.explanation: The largest partition fell from 204 to 122 rows while the join still returned 240 rows and the same regional totals. The cost is a twelve-row dimension, two exchanges on the new key and a plan the next reader must understand.

cards.prompt: What does isFinalPlan=false tell you about an adaptive plan you just printed?
cards.answer: That no action has run yet: adaptive execution finalizes the plan only after it measures shuffle output, so the printed exchanges and partition counts may still change.
cards.explanation: After its action the grouped plan read isFinalPlan=true with AQEShuffleRead coalesced, and one task read all twelve partial records instead of four tasks. Print the plan again after the action to see what actually ran.

cards.prompt: State one thing the recorded local run proves and one thing it cannot.
cards.answer: It proves exchange counts, executed stages and tasks, shuffle records and where rows landed for Spark 4.0.4 in local[2]; it cannot prove any duration, memory use, spill or cluster behaviour.
cards.explanation: Each experiment changed one setting on 240 rows in one configuration. A statement such as broadcast is always faster or raise shuffle partitions needs measurements at the real size, on the real runtime, with the real key distribution.

cards.prompt: Interpret this: six identical adaptive runs built BuildLeft twice and BuildRight four times.
cards.answer: Which side adaptive execution broadcasts is a runtime outcome of that run, not a property of the query, so a single run's side is not evidence about sizes.
cards.explanation: Spark converts a sort-merge join when the runtime statistics of any join side qualify; with both input shuffles running at once, the order they finish is the likely reason the side varied. The lab records the sides and asserts only that the strategy switched.

cards.prompt: Why did adaptive skew handling leave the 204-row join partition alone at its defaults?
cards.answer: A partition counts as skewed only when it exceeds five times the median partition size and 256 MB; a few kilobytes of shuffle is nowhere near that.
cards.explanation: With the threshold and advisory size scaled to 1 KB on the record, the plan read SortMergeJoin(skew=true) and three tasks read 102, 106 and 37 records instead of one reading 206. That demonstrates the mechanism; it is not a setting to copy.

cards.prompt: After cache() and one count(), what does the next grouped plan change and what does it keep?
cards.answer: Its input becomes InMemoryTableScan over InMemoryRelation; the Exchange for the grouping key and every count stay exactly as before.
cards.explanation: Caching changes where rows come from, not how they must move: grouping by line still needs hashpartitioning(line#2, 4). Counts stayed L1 64, L2 63, L3 53, and unpersist() returned the plan to a scan and filter.

cards.prompt: Why can count() not exhaust driver memory while collect() on the same frame can?
cards.answer: count() returns one number from partial counts computed by the tasks; collect() serializes every row and sends all of them to the one driver process.
cards.explanation: The driver is one process with one heap. The lab's guard counted limit(51) first and refused the raw frame at a bound of 50 rows, while count() reported 240 without moving a row to the driver.
